advances: Disproves uniqueness for unrestricted centroids of strict quadrilateral sections with a fixed split.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
The roots $x,y=(1-2z\pm\sqrt{1-8z})/2$ are distinct and positive, since their product and sum are positive. Apply the diagonal parametrization from tetrahedral-quadrilateral-section-calculus. Because $(x+z)(y+z)=xy+z(x+y)+z^2=2z$, the centroid coordinate at index $0$ obeys
$$
3\lambda_0=x\left(\frac{2}{x+z}-1\right)=1+z.
$$
For the last equality, $(1+z+x)(x+z)=2x$ follows by substituting $x^2=(1-2z)x-z-z^2$. The same calculation gives $\lambda_1=(1+z)/3$, and symmetry and the sum to one give $\lambda_2=\lambda_3=(1-2z)/6$. Swapping $x,y$ preserves that centroid. In the third diagonal point $A+B=1/2$, so each of its centroid coordinates equals its diagonal coordinate by the same formula. The three points differ because $x\ne y$, and the diagonal bijection gives distinct planes. At $z=3/25$ the first two diagonal points are $(12,7,3,3)/25$ and $(7,12,3,3)/25$, and the centroid is $(56,56,19,19)/150$. Substitution of these rational data into the reciprocal-height, cap, and moment formulas gives the displayed values.

source_sections.locator: §1, symmetric three-plane pencil for p in (0,1/3)

statement: Fix a tetrahedron and the split $\{0,1\}\mid\{2,3\}$. For every $0<z<1/8$, take distinct positive $x,y$ with $x+y=1-2z$ and $xy=z+z^2$. The three strict quadrilateral planes whose diagonal intersections are $(x,y,z,z)$, $(y,x,z,z)$, and $(A,A,B,B)$, where $A=(1+z)/3$, $B=(1-2z)/6$, all have actual section centroid $(A,A,B,B)$. At $z=3/25$ their oriented raw heights can be taken as $(7,12,-28,-28),(12,7,-28,-28),(19,19,-56,-56)$, and each of the first two caps has fraction $4/25$ and normalized scalar moment $-111/400$ toward the ordinary tetrahedral centroid.
title: Three distinct quadrilateral planes with the same tetrahedral section centroid
